title: Traditional Maori Fish Hooks

paragraphs.text: Effective fish hooks were used by Maori to harvest the rich fisheries of New Zealand, but after the introduction of metals by Europeans they were quickly discarded. The nature of the designs, their function and unrecognised benefits were lost, and subsequently many hooks were incorrectly interpreted as decorative, ceremonial or superstitious objects. So it is ironic that internationally many commercial fishermen now regard circle hooks as a recent innovation, even though they were the preferred design used by Maori a millennium ago.

Maori, who had always been great fishermen, first sailed to New Zealand from the Pacific islands around 1100 AD. However, in the new country they found different types of wood, bone and stone from those they were familiar with from the tropical Pacific islands, so they set about adapting and revising the skills they used to fabricate the hooks – known as ‘matau’ – and other tackle needed to harvest fish. It has also been found that New Zealand plants such as flax, cabbage tree and astelia provided fibrous material for fishing lines and nets that was equal to, or superior to, the jute, hemp and sisal in use by Europeans at the time. But unlike metals that can be forged or bent into any desired shape, the materials available to Maori imposed limitations on hook design because of the nature of their structure, and compromises were necessary.

The first European explorers in New Zealand often observed local fishing techniques and seem to have come into possession of some fishing equipment, as various hooks were returned to Europe and displayed. The explorers, however, were not overly impressed, writing that Maori hooks were ‘odd’, ‘of doubtful efficacy’, or ‘very clumsy affairs’. Even recent archaeologists have commented that the traditional hook was 'shaped in a manner which looks most ineffective for catching fish'. William Anderson, the surgeon on board the Resolution during Captain Cook’s third voyage to New Zealand in 1777, remarked on the great productivity of Maori intensive agriculture, but was perplexed by their ‘wooden fish hooks pointed with bone, which are so oddly made that a stranger cannot understand how they can be successful.’

Two hundred and thirty years later, a study of Maori fish hooks undertaken by Victoria University showed that the unusual design was related to how the hooks functioned – catching fish by rotating away from the direction of the point and becoming wedged under the jaw, rather than penetrating the side of the fish’s mouth in the manner of a European hook, or by acting as a lever as proposed by some archaeologists.

Maori were quick to adopt new materials that became available after the arrival of Europeans in the late 1700s. They continued to make fish hooks according to their traditional designs, but used the new metals and imported fibres. The more commonplace traditional hooks were either thrown away, after which the wooden and flax components soon decomposed, or were used to acquire blankets or medicines from Europeans, with the result that a regular trade developed. More highly prized fish hooks made from ivory or greenstone were often retained and used for jewellery, and today stylised fish hooks are seen as a symbol of Maori cultural revival.

But despite the arrival of new materials, Maori continued to replicate traditional forms in preference to hook shapes introduced by Europeans well into the late 1800s. Eventually, however, the extraordinary quantity of mass-produced metal European hooks being brought into the country led to a significant reduction in their cost, making them irresistible to Maori. This, and the difficulty of manufacturing traditional designs from nails and the other metal objects available to Maori, diminished the use of traditional designs. However, in the late 1900s, the increasing demand for Maori artefacts in Europe, in particular from collectors who were fascinated by Pacific cultures, led to heightened interest in fish hooks. One consequence of this was the increasing incidence of Maori manufacturing fake hooks for sale into this lucrative market. These can usually be identified by the quality of their construction and carving, or by the materials used.

In many ways the evolution of Maori fish hooks mirrors the way in which Maori adapted many European materials and technologies to their own purpose. European influence and technology added to, rather than replaced, generally compatible Maori techniques. This is relevant to fish hooks but also many other aspects of Maori life, in particular the development of various tools, where customary materials were replaced or complemented by metals and, more recently, synthetic materials. Today, commercial boats around the world have adopted a circular hook design because it has proved more effective. Closer inspection shows that these hooks are almost identical in form and function to the traditional matau – technology preferred by Maori since their arrival in New Zealand.
